data: Roscosmos / Soviet Academy of Sciences (lead, IKI) — international payload from ESA / CNES / Hungary / Austria / Bulgaria / Czechoslovakia / Poland / East Germany

About 4900 kg in total, including the ~1500 kg descent module (Venera-type lander + first-of-kind helium balloon aerostat). Twin spacecraft Vega 1 / Vega 2 launched 6 days apart for the same Venus-then-Halley itinerary.

© Roscosmos / IKI / international consortium. Vega 1 lifted off from Baikonur 1984-12-15 carrying a Soviet Venus lander descended from the Venera line plus a helium aerostat (balloon) built by CNES with IKI — the first balloon deployment in another planet's atmosphere. The descent module separated 1985-06-09 and entered Venus's atmosphere 1985-06-11. The balloon drifted at ~54 km altitude for 46.5 hours, transmitting wind + temperature data via a 20-station global radio network. The bus, freed of its descent mass, used Venus gravity assist to redirect to comet 1P/Halley, achieving closest approach (8890 km) on 1986-03-06 — three days ahead of Vega 2, and 8 days ahead of ESA's Giotto, which used Vega's flyby position fix to navigate its own 596 km Halley flyby. This made Vega 1 the first spacecraft to visit both a planet and a comet (Mariner 10 had visited two planets).

Baikonur Cosmodrome, 1984-12-15. Soviet dual-target mission — "Vega" combines VEnera + GAlley (Halley) in Russian transliteration. Two identical spacecraft (Vega 1 + 2) used Venus gravity to redirect toward comet Halley after deploying landers + balloons in Venus's atmosphere.

1985-06-11. Vega 1 released a lander (touched down at Mermaid Plains) and a helium balloon (drifted at 54 km altitude for 47 hours, the first atmospheric balloon at another planet). Vega 1 itself flew on past Venus, using the gravity assist to redirect toward Halley.

Closest approach 8,890 km from Halley's nucleus on 1986-03-06 — the first images of a comet's nucleus, 8 days before Giotto's much closer pass. Vega's camera images of the nucleus, with VLBI tracking of Vega's position, refined Giotto's aim point (the 'Pathfinder' scheme): "the Halley Armada" cooperative tracking enabled Giotto to safely fly to 596 km without an unknown nucleus position.
First-ever balloon aerostat deployed in another planet's atmosphere (Venus, 1985); first spacecraft to visit both a planet and a comet

Soviet flagship of the Halley armada. Vega 1 launched 1984-12-15 with a Venera-lineage lander plus a first-of-kind helium balloon built by CNES with IKI that drifted in Venus's cloud deck at 54 km altitude for 46.5 hours, transmitting wind + temperature data via a 20-station global radio net. After dropping its descent module the bus used Venus gravity assist to redirect to comet 1P/Halley, achieving a 8890 km closest approach on 1986-03-06 — the first images of a comet's nucleus, and the position fix that ESA's Giotto used to navigate its own much closer Halley flyby 8 days later.
